overlap.title: What became of Shiloh, and of the house of the Lord there, after “the ark of God was taken”?
overlap.summary: In 1 Samuel 1–4 the yearly worship, Eli’s priesthood and the ark are at Shiloh. The ark is taken in battle and a runner brings the news to Shiloh. The compared passages do not narrate what happened to the sanctuary at Shiloh: the returned ark goes to Kirjathjearim, and priests with the shewbread are later described at Nob. Jeremiah says “see what I did to it” and a psalm says God “forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh”. The verses compared do not say what was done to Shiloh, when, or by whom.
overlap.reasoning: Shiloh is where the tabernacle was set up (Joshua 18:1) and where the first chapters of 1 Samuel place the sacrifices, the priests and the ark. The cited scene at Shiloh reports the arrival of news that the ark was taken (4:12 and the verses after it). When the ark comes back it is not brought to Shiloh, and priests with the shewbread are later at Nob. Jeremiah points to Shiloh as a place where something was done that his hearers could go and see, and makes it the pattern for what will be done to the house in Jerusalem; Psalm 78 says God forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh. None of the verses compared narrates that event. What it was, and whether it followed the battle of 1 Samuel 4 or came later, bears on how the later priestly setting at Nob, the separate resting place of the ark and Jeremiah’s warning are read; these verses do not directly narrate a move of the priesthood from Shiloh to Nob.
overlap.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the Philistines destroyed Shiloh after the battle; that the place was left by the priests without being destroyed, and that what Jeremiah speaks of happened at a later time; that the forsaking in Psalm 78 is the loss of the ark and nothing more. Limits: Jeremiah 7:12 says something was done to “my place which was in Shiloh” because of wickedness and does not say what, when, or by whose hand; Psalms 78:60–61 joins the forsaking of the tabernacle of Shiloh to the delivering of “his strength into captivity” and does not describe the place afterwards; 1 Kings 14:2 and Jeremiah 41:5 speak of people at or from Shiloh in later times, so the verses quoted do not show the place empty for ever; at 1 Samuel 14:3 the words “the Lord's priest in Shiloh” may describe Eli and not Ahiah, and the verse does not say the priesthood was still at Shiloh in Saul’s time; 1 Samuel calls the house at Shiloh “the temple of the Lord” (1:9) and “the tabernacle of the congregation” (2:22), and whether the tabernacle later said to be at Gibeon (2 Chronicles 1:3) was moved from Shiloh, and when, is not told in the verses quoted; Brenton’s Greek of 2:22, quoted in full above, has no clause about the women or the tabernacle, a wording difference stated here and not proposed as a separate finding. Check made: a whole-word search of the packaged KJV for “Shiloh” finds, in 1 Samuel, 1:3, 1:9, 1:24, 2:14, 3:21, 4:3, 4:4, 4:12 and 14:3, and after 1 Samuel, 1 Kings 2:27, 14:2 and 14:4, Psalms 78:60, and Jeremiah 7:12, 7:14, 26:6, 26:9 and 41:5; each of those verses was read in the KJV, with 1 Samuel 4:3–4, 4:10–22, 7:1–2, 21:1–6 and 22:9–19; 1 Samuel 2:22 and 14:3 were also read in the Hebrew and the Greek. That is a word search and a reading of those verses, not a reading of the whole Bible, and a passage that tells of Shiloh without naming it would not be found by it. These checked verses do not explicitly settle what was done to Shiloh or when. No H or G is proposed. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

studies.title: Can God be seen?
studies.summary: Exodus describes Moses speaking with God “face to face”; John says no one has seen God. The tension depends on whether “face to face” means literal sight.

studies.title: Judas and the field of blood
studies.summary: Matthew and Acts give different accounts of Judas's death and the field purchase.

studies.title: Water or ground: the animals’ origin
studies.summary: Genesis 1 can sound like birds came from water, while Genesis 2 says ground. The apparent conflict depends on how Genesis 1:20 is translated.

studies.title: Plants before people—or after?
studies.summary: Genesis 1 places vegetation before people; Genesis 2 describes no field plants before a cultivator. Whether this conflicts depends on which plants are meant.

studies.title: David’s census: two different totals
studies.summary: The census totals differ: Israel is 800,000 versus 1.1 million; Judah is 500,000 versus 470,000. Different counting rules are proposed but not established here.

studies.title: Herod, Quirinius, and the birth chronology
studies.summary: Matthew places Jesus’s birth under Herod; Luke links it to Quirinius’s census. The historical chronology creates a tension if the same census is intended.
